claim: The worldwide prevalence of obesity has more than doubled in the last thirty years.
source: the worldwide prevalence of obesity has more than doubled in the last thirty years, making it one of the most important global public health challenges (Yatsuya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yatsuya et al., 2014

claim: Obesity is a preventable risk factor for cardiovascular and metabolic disorders such as heart disease and type-2 diabetes.
source: Obesity has long been recognised as a preventable risk factor for cardiovascular and metabolic disorders such as heart disease and type-2 diabetes.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus

claim: Obesity is an important risk factor for neurodegenerative disorders, linked to both an increased risk of dementia and accelerated age-associated cognitive decline.
source: More recently, it has also emerged as an important risk factor for neurodegenerative disorders, linked to both an increased risk of dementia and accelerated age-associated cognitive decline (Sellbom and Gunstad, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sellbom and Gunstad, 2012

claim: Obesity is defined as the excessive accumulation of adipose tissue in the body.
source: Defined as the excessive accumulation of adipose tissue in the body (González-Muniesa et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Muniesa et al., 2017

claim: Studies investigating effects of obesity on the brain have focused almost exclusively on macroscopic aspects of brain structure such as total grey matter volume and cortical thickness.
source: To date, cross-sectional and longitudinal studies investigating effects of obesity on the brain have focused almost exclusively on macroscopic aspects of brain structure such as total grey matter volume and cortical thickness.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Results in the field of obesity and brain structure were often contradictory, with studies tending to report lower gray matter volume in relation to obesity, but some also observing null or positive associations.
source: Results in this field were often contradictory: although studies tended to report lower gray matter volume in relation to obesity, some have also observed null or positive associations as described in a meta-analysis by García-García et al., 2019
evidence: Supported by citation to García-García et al., 2019 meta-analysis

claim: The likely reasons for contradictory results in obesity-brain studies were heterogeneities in brain and obesity metrics, a wide variation in sample size, and poor statistical methodology.
source: as described in a meta-analysis by García-García et al., 2019, who noted that the likely reasons for this were heterogeneities in brain and obesity metrics, a wide variation in sample size, and poor statistical methodology.
evidence: Supported by citation to García-García et al., 2019

claim: The emerging consensus indicates that studies are reporting negative associations between obesity (particularly visceral obesity indexed by waist to hip ratio: WHR) and (smaller) total grey matter volume.
source: However, the emerging consensus indicates that typically studies are reporting negative associations between obesity (particularly visceral obesity indexed by waist to hip ratio: WHR) and (smaller) total grey matter volume (Cox et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cox et al., 2019

claim: The emerging consensus indicates that studies are reporting negative associations between obesity and (thinner) cortical thickness.
source: However, the emerging consensus indicates that typically studies are reporting negative associations between obesity (particularly visceral obesity indexed by waist to hip ratio: WHR) and (smaller) total grey matter volume (Cox et al., 2019) and (thinner) cortical thickness (Caunca et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caunca et al., 2019

claim: The negative association between body mass index (BMI) and global grey matter volume has been substantiated in a recent large-scale study conducted in the UK Biobank involving 9652 participants.
source: Notably, this negative association between body mass index (BMI) and global grey matter volume has been substantiated in a recent large-scale study conducted in the UK Biobank involving 9652 participants (Hamer and Batty, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamer and Batty, 2019

claim: Recent meta-analysis of voxel-based morphometry studies, including data from 5882 participants and a mega-analysis of 6,420 participants from the ENIGMA MDD working group, have identified a consistent association of obesity with reductions in grey matter volume and cortical thickness in the medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex and the temporal pole.
source: Recent meta-analysis of voxel-based morphometry studies, including data from 5882 participants and a mega-analysis of 6,420 participants from the ENIGMA MDD working group, have also identified a consistent association of obesity with reductions in grey matter volume and cortical thickness in the medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex and the temporal pole (García-García et al., 2022; Opel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to García-García et al., 2022 and Opel et al., 2021

claim: Franz et al. showed that by the age of 64 years, participants whose BMI steadily increased over forty years had thinner cortex in several frontal and temporal brain regions compared to those whose BMI was stable.
source: For example, Franz et al. showed that by the age of 64 years, participants whose BMI steadily increased over forty years had thinner cortex in several frontal and temporal brain regions compared to those whose BMI was stable (Franz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Franz et al., 2019

claim: Longitudinal studies have shown associations between age-associated increases in BMI and grey matter reductions in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal cortex and hippocampus) and cingulate cortex.
source: Other longitudinal studies have shown associations between age-associated increases in BMI and grey matter reductions in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal cortex and hippocampus) and cingulate cortex (Arnoldussen et al., 2019; Bobb et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arnoldussen et al., 2019 and Bobb et al., 2014

claim: There is a significant age-by-obesity interaction on cortical thickness driven by lower thickness in older participants.
source: Together with the finding (Opel et al., 2021) of a significant age-by-obesity interaction on cortical thickness driven by lower thickness in older participants
evidence: Supported by citation to Opel et al., 2021

claim: The negative impact of obesity on the brain accumulates over time.
source: this suggests that the negative impact of obesity on the brain accumulates over time.
evidence: Inferred from longitudinal studies and age-by-obesity interaction findings

claim: There is robust evidence for an association between obesity and macro-structural features of brain anatomy such as grey matter volume and cortical thickness.
source: Together, these studies provide robust evidence for an association between obesity and macro-structural features of brain anatomy such as grey matter volume and cortical thickness.
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple cited studies

claim: Our understanding of the microstructural features that underpin the relationship between obesity and brain structure remain largely unknown.
source: However, changes in grey matter volume and cortical thickness can be driven by multiple different underlying processes and our understanding of the microstructural features that underpin this relationship remain largely unknown (Westwater et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Westwater et al., 2022

claim: It is currently not known whether obesity-associated differences in grey matter volume relate to changes in the size, shape or number of neurons, neurite density or orientation dispersion, or alternately to differences in tissue water content.
source: For example, it is currently not known whether obesity-associated differences in grey matter volume relate to changes in the size, shape or number of neurons e.g. neurite density or orientation dispersion within that region or alternately to differences in tissue water content.
evidence: Statement about current knowledge gap

claim: Studies investigating associations of obesity with brain microstructure have focused on white matter.
source: To date, the only studies to have investigated associations of obesity with brain microstructure have focused on white matter.

claim: Studies have identified obesity-associated differences in white matter including obesity-related increases in white matter water content, reduced myelination, and lower fractional anisotropy.
source: Interestingly, these have identified obesity-associated differences in a number of different microstructural features of white matter including (1) obesity-related increases in white matter water content, (2) reduced myelination, and (3) lower fractional anisotropy (Zhang et al., 2018; Kullmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2018 and Kullmann et al., 2016

claim: Whether comparable differences in cortical and subcortical grey matter micro-structure can be observed with obesity are yet to be reported.
source: However, whether comparable differences in cortical and subcortical grey matter micro-structure can be observed with obesity are yet to be reported.
evidence: Statement about current knowledge gap

claim: The study used data from approximately 30,000 participants in the UK Biobank MRI cohort.
source: We hypothesized that obesity would be associated with diffusion-MRI measures of grey matter tissue microstructure at 180 cortical regions and 8 subcortical structures (bilaterally) produced using neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) modelling of data from ∼30,000 participants in the UK Biobank MRI cohort.

claim: NODDI requires data collected at multiple different diffusion weightings (shells).
source: Unlike conventional diffusion MRI which models data acquired at a single diffusion weighting (shell), NODDI requires data collected at multiple different diffusion weightings (shells)

claim: In the NODDI model, diffusion is modelled as isotropic in free water, restricted within neurites, and hindered in the extracellular space.
source: In this model, diffusion is modelled as isotropic in free water, restricted within neurites, and hindered in the extracellular space

source: Intracellular Volume Fraction (ICVF), which captures the volume fraction occupied by neurites (axons and dendrites) but not cell bodies
evidence: Definition of ICVF metric

claim: Orientation Dispersion Index (OD) captures the spatial distribution of neurites.
source: Orientation Dispersion Index (OD), which captures the spatial distribution of these processes

source: For example, FA, OD, and ICVF metrics of neurite density were more strongly correlated with each other than with ISOVF

claim: There were areas of significant negative correlation between ISOVF and WHR in the lateral and medial secondary visual cortex.
source: There were also some areas of significant negative correlation between ISOVF and WHR in the lateral and medial secondary visual cortex (see Figure 1b).

claim: Neurite density (ICVF) was significantly positively correlated with WHR (FDR = 5%) in 152 bilateral regions concentrated in a medial temporal-occipital-striatal system.
source: In contrast, neurite density (ICVF) was significantly positively correlated with WHR (FDR = 5%) in 152 bilateral regions concentrated in a medial temporal-occipital-striatal system comprising medial and lateral occipital cortex (26 regions), medial temporal lobe (hippocampus and amygdala), basal ganglia (putamen, pallidum, accumbens), hypothalamus and thalamus (see Figure 1d).

claim: The anatomical pattern of ICVF~WHR has previously been activated by fMRI tasks involving episodic memory and navigation.

source: This suggests that obesity is associated with coupled but anatomically distinct changes in measures of brain water and neurite density.

source: The prefrontal-temporal-striatal system (ISOVF~WHR) was significantly (positively) co-located with the atlas distribution of five neurotransmitter receptors/transporters: 5HTT, serotonin transporter; D1, dopamine receptor; H3, histamine receptor; Mu, opioid receptor; and VAChT, acetyl-choline transporter.
